Two samples of a directionally solidified Al-26wt%Cu were coarsened at 5°C above the aluminum liquidus temperature (553°C) for duration of 10 minutes and 5 days (Fig. 5, Fig. 6). The samples were then serial sectioned at 4.75 μm intervals to a total of 100 sections and digitally reconstructed. The phase pictured represents solid Al, while the encompassing eutectic liquid phase has been set to total transparence for viewing ease. The solid phase accounts for a 40% volume fraction of the sample.
Fig. 5 Three-dimensional reconstruction of a 10 minute coarsened sample of Al-26wt%Cu from 100 serial sections at 4.75μm increments
Fig. 6 Three-dimensional reconstruction of a 5 day coarsened sample of Al-26wt%Cu from 100 serial sections at 4.75μm increments

On initial inspection, it is clear that the sample coarsened for 10 minutes is extremely interconnected, complex and dense in the solid Al orientation (Fig. 5). Such a configuration would be expected to yield surface orientations and curvatures across the entire spectrum. For instance, it is clear that surface normals placed randomly throughout the sample would be positioned in almost every possible direction. Furthermore, the visibly diverse range of dendritic shapes is expected to yield a wide range of curvature measures. On the other hand, the sample coarsened for 5 days (Fig. 6) is much less dense in solid packing, and the dendritic shapes have undergone a visually evident change in length scale. A more limited distribution of normal vectors and surface curvatures would be expected for this microstructure.

Figure 7 shows the stereographically projected, orientation density plots for the 10 minute sample created through IDL. The figure presents the two hemispheres of the reference sphere projected around both the positive z-axis (the growth direction) and the negative z-axis (refer to Fig. 2). Most clearly illustrated by the plot is the broad range of surface orientations present throughout the microstructure, which is seen in Figure 5. Furthermore, there are clearly four localized density regions projected about the z-axis. This observation signifies that there is in fact a general directionality present in the system with respect to the growth direction. The projection planes of a microstructure with limited or no directionality, such as the sphere in Figure 9, would yield a uniform density of poles throughout both hemispheres. Moreover, the particular arrangement of orientation density peaks illustrates almost perfect four-fold symmetry. Such symmetry is expected in an unvaryingly complex and interconnected microstructure of limited or no coarsening.
